title: Tu BiShvat: a seder of fruits
hookLine: the Safed mystics made a seder of fruits and four cups of wine

cards: It begins as a line in a tax code. The Mishnah lists four new years in the Jewish calendar, and one is for trees. Why do trees need a new year?
Because the Torah's tithes and fruit laws count a tree's age, and someone has to decide when its year turns over.
The schools of Shammai and Hillel disagreed about the date, and Hillel's view won: the fifteenth of the month of Shevat. In Hebrew numbers, fifteen is written tet-vav, said tu. Tu BiShvat.
For a long time, it was mostly a date for bookkeeping. Then a group of mystics sat down at a table and turned it into a feast.

teach.b: The mystics were kabbalists in the tradition of Safed, the hill town in the Galilee where a circle of Jewish mystics gathered. Their followers wrote a little book, later printed as Pri Etz Hadar, fruit of the goodly tree.
It lays out a Tu BiShvat seder, an ordered meal like Passover's, but made of fruit. First, the fruits of the Land of Israel.

The Torah praises the land, in the old Jewish translation, as "a land of wheat and barley, and vines and fig-trees and pomegranates; a land of olive-trees and honey." The rabbis read that honey as date honey.
Seven species, and the seder makes sure to eat them.
Then the fruits are sorted into three groups: a hard shell outside, like walnuts and pomegranates; a hard pit inside, like olives and dates; and ones you can eat completely, like figs and grapes.
For the mystics, these stood for layers of the world, from the most guarded to the most open.
Then four cups of wine: white, then white with a little red, then mostly red, then all red. Some read it as winter warming into spring.
A blessing is said over each new fruit, with passages from the Bible and the Zohar read between. Today families, schools and environmental groups hold Tu BiShvat seders, some traditional, some new.
At the heart of the old order is a simple act: paying attention to what grows on a tree, and saying a blessing before eating it.

how: Many Jews eat fruits of the Land of Israel on Tu BiShvat, especially the seven species, and some hold a Tu BiShvat seder following the kabbalists' order of fruits and four cups of wine moving from white to red.

o: the spring day the first fruits are brought
the autumn day the harvest is gathered in

games.q: inside the seder of fruits — tap the pairs.

s: Tu BiShvat began as a date in the Mishnah's list of new years
the new year for trees, used to count a tree's age for tithes and fruit laws.
the four cups of the Tu BiShvat seder are all red
they move from white, to white with red, to mostly red, to all red.
the Torah itself describes the Tu BiShvat seder
the seder came from kabbalists in the tradition of Safed, many centuries later.

games.q: Shammai's school and Hillel's school disagree about the date of the new year for trees. whose date became Tu BiShvat?
games.why: Hillel's school said the fifteenth, and that became the day: tu, fifteen, in Shevat.

practice: If you have fruit nearby, set out up to three kinds, one with a peel, one with a pit, one you can eat whole; if not, picture them.
Look at one properly, its color, its weight, the tree it came from, and if you say blessings, this is a moment for one. Then eat slowly, noticing how each is different.

wordCard.voice: Tu BiShvat. The fifteenth of Shevat, the new year for trees, and for the mystics, a seder of fruits and four cups. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the fifteenth of Shevat. tet-vav, nine plus six, is how fifteen is written.
